waypoints.name: SR-20 Wine Spires pullout (milepost 166)
waypoints.note: Unmarked highway pullout ~2-4 miles east of the Washington Pass hairpin turn; climbers descend to Early Winters Creek then switchback up to Burgundy Col.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the unsigned pullout near milepost 166, roughly four miles east of Washington Pass, at about 4,300 ft. There is no sign and no developed trailhead here, only a broad shoulder pullout, so watch your odometer. Check WSDOT before travelling: the highway is gated shut through the winter and reopens somewhere between mid-April and late June depending on snowpack and slide repair.

waypoints.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Burgundy Col
waypoints.directions: From the pullout, drop off the highway on a steep, faint boot path and descend the talus to Early Winters Creek, crossing on logs. Climb the far side on the climber's path, switchbacking up talus benches and loose cairned gullies through timber and boulders; where the boot track braids, stay climber's-left, keeping north of the drainage coming down from the basin below the spires, and aim for the obvious notch of the col. It is about 3,500 ft of gain and 3-4 hours with an overnight pack, and snow can linger in the gully below the col into July, so carry an axe early in the season.

waypoints.name: Chianti Spire / East Face (Rebel Yell) area
waypoints.directions: Drop off the col down a short snow and rock step and traverse south beneath the east face of Burgundy Spire, crossing a small snowy rib onto the upper Silver Star Glacier, then around to the obvious east side of Chianti Spire at about 7,900 ft. Reckon on under an hour from the col, or from the larch bench camp lower down. Carry an ice axe through midsummer, as the rib and the glacier margin are often firm or icy first thing in the morning.

waypoints.name: Chianti Spire Summit
waypoints.directions: Seven pitches of gear-protected crack climbing up the east face, four to six hours for most parties. Start up flakes into the obvious wide dihedral, taking either the easier right-hand start or the thinner left-hand finger crack, which rejoins by the top of pitch 1, then the offwidth and the lower-angle dihedral above, then the balancy blind step left across the arete past a fixed bolt on pitch 4. Pitch 5 is the technical crux, a sustained thin-hands crack widening through cupped hands to fists and capped by a strenuous offwidth move, and pitch 6 follows the same system to a rising ramp trending left to the exposed summit block, gained by short final moves past a single bolt.

expect.approach: The North Fork Sauk approach starts from the unsigned Sloan Peak climbers'-trail pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road, reached via SR 530 south of Darrington) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk River — not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649, but a boot path a short distance further along FR 49. From the pullout the path is flat and brushy (stinging nettle, then devil's club) for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the North Fork Sauk River, which must be forded or crossed on logs (log jams are usually adequate about 0.5 mi in; they shift year to year and can be dicey in high water/early season). The path fords the river braids two to three times over the next mile, then follows Cougar Creek upstream on a faint, cairned/flagged track through sandy streambed and forest — expect route-finding to be slow here, especially with snow on the ground into early summer. Around 3,000–3,200 ft the trail crosses Cougar Creek itself (can be impassable lower down; look for a crossing around 3.2K ft) and climbs steeply through switchbacks in forest, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft (roughly 2–2.5 hrs from the car, and the last reliable water before the basin). Above the falls the climbers' path breaks out of the trees onto scree and slabs, angling up to the 5,800 ft saddle/basin on Sloan's northeast side (reached ~4–5 hrs in for most parties), with a small stream and possible campsite in the basin — the standard overnight/base camp spot for a two-day ascent. From the basin, ledges and slabs lead up to the toe of the Sloan Glacier; rope up and gear up (crampons, axe, glacier kit) here before crossing onto the ice toward the southeast edge of the summit massif. The often-preferred approach uses the Bedal Creek trailhead (FS 4096, a rough 3-mile 4WD spur off the Mountain Loop Highway, ~2,790 ft) and the old Bedal Creek trail/climbers' path to the same 5,300 ft Bedal–Sloan saddle, avoiding the North Fork Sauk fords entirely at the cost of a rougher access road; total stats by that line run about 9.5 mi and 5,300 ft round trip. Either way, expect avalanche/snow-slope hazard on the basin and glacier approach into early summer, one notable open crevasse on the Sloan Glacier that's typically snow-bridged in normal season, and generally loose, brushy, unmaintained tread below treeline on both approaches. Most parties now come in by the Bedal Creek trail instead: the road up to it is potholed with one washed-out stretch near the top, so bring high clearance, and from the upper parking head straight into the forest rather than up the logging spur to the right (in early July the first mile is choked with blowdown and brush).

set.approach: Most parties start from the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,800 ft, at the end of a rough high-clearance spur (Forest Road 4096) off the Mountain Loop Highway a mile or so past the Bedal campground. Follow the Bedal Creek trail through old-growth forest and along the creek to where a large washout has taken the tread; scramble the washout to a cairned exit, then climb the climbers' path through forest and onto talus and meadow to the saddle near 5,300 ft, the last dependable water. From there bear toward the moraine and the lower glacier. A second, less used approach starts from the pullout on Sloan Creek Road and fords the North Fork Sauk River, then follows Cougar Creek; it avoids the Bedal road, but the crossings are dangerous in high water, mainly May through July.

expect.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. From the summit, downclimb the same Class 2 (right side) or Class 2/3 (center) slope back down about 600 vertical feet to the ~5,000 ft bench, then reverse the counterclockwise talus traverse below the cliff bands back to treeline, and continue down through open forest and brush to the FR-6517 parking area. No technical anchors or rappels are needed on the standard line. The main descent hazards are loose talus/scree (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below) and route-finding — in poor visibility it's easy to drift toward the cliff bands instead of holding the correct counterclockwise line, so retrace your ascent traverse carefully. Parties who climbed the more exposed far-left finish (about 50 ft of slightly exposed Class 3) sometimes downclimb that section more cautiously or carry ~50 ft of rope to rig an optional handline for extra security, but this is a personal-comfort choice on a minor variation, not a fixed rappel station, and the standard Class 2/3 line requires no rope at all. Parties in September and July used a short rappel (about 15-30 m) from a tree above the cliff band, or the fixed rope found at the steep forest bypass, to get down the crux section safely.
pro_tips: Identify the correct gully/ramp on the north side before committing — the right side is easier Class 2, the center/left is Class 2/3 and more exposed
Bring a map/GPS track for the NE-to-N counterclockwise talus traverse; it's easy to end up on the wrong side of the cliffs in the forest
Call the Skykomish Ranger Station or check MBS current-conditions page for FR65/6510/6514/6517 status before driving — these spur roads see periodic washout/shoulder damage
Carry a 50 ft handline for the exposed Class 3 downclimb on the north side rather than downclimbing it unroped
Best after the north-facing summit gully clears of snow for secure scrambling
Put on microspikes before the cliff band and the steep duff above it; they help on the way down too.
In mid-August the line was marked with blue ribbons through the gully above the lower cliff band; bring a hand line for the short scramble up to it.
gear: 50 ft handline (optional, for the Class 3 downclimb)

set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line. The one place that is not a plain walk-off is the lower cliff band on the north side, roughly 15 m of slabby rock and loose dirt. In dry weather it downclimbs at class 3; wet, mossy or snowy it is closer to class 4 and most parties rope it. Walk the steep forest above it, belay off a tree just above the band, and make a single rappel of about 15 m (a 30 m rope with a sling and a rappel ring covers it). Do not rely on rope or webbing left on the slope by earlier parties. Below the band, continue the talus traverse back to treeline and the road end.

Bring a 30 m rope, a sling and a rappel ring for the lower cliff band on the north side; it is class 3 dry but class 4 when wet, and a short rappel from a tree above it is the usual way down.
